etymology: Dutch Reformed theologian (1636-1708), author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.
biblical_def: Herman Witsius was a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor, one of the most learned and irenic divines of the Further Reformation, best known for his masterwork The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man. In it he set out the whole plan of salvation under the framework of the covenants: the covenant of works made with Adam, broken by the fall, and the covenant of grace established in Christ, with the eternal covenant of redemption between the Father and the Son as its foundation. Witsius held together what lesser men divided — rigorous doctrine and warm experiential piety, careful scholarship and tender devotion. He labored as a peacemaker in the bitter disputes between the so-called antinomians and neonomians, seeking to honor both free grace and the necessity of holiness without surrendering either to error. His writing is marked by reverence, balance, and a deep savor of communion with God. Witsius stands in the dictionary as the great expositor of covenant theology, who taught the church to read the whole of Scripture as the unfolding of God's covenant dealings, and who joined the precision of the scholastic to the warmth of the godly heart.
webster_summary: Dutch Reformed theologian (1636-1708), author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man; a learned and irenic divine who joined rigorous covenant theology to warm experiential piety.

corruption_summary: Witsius's legacy is honored by recovering covenant theology as the framework of Scripture and by refuting the caricature of Reformed scholasticism as cold, against an age that severs doctrine from devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: Dead-orthodoxy caricature. Reformed scholastics like Witsius are often dismissed as dry and lifeless, their precision mistaken for coldness. Witsius himself refutes the slander: his covenant theology breathes reverence and communion, and his learning served piety, not pride. The dictionary holds that sound doctrine and warm devotion are not enemies; the most exact theology, rightly held, kindles the deepest love for God, and Witsius is a model of the union the church must recover.

Covenant-flattened misreading. Some read Scripture as a loose collection of stories and rules, missing the covenantal structure that binds it into one redemptive plan. Witsius recovers the unity: from the covenant of works with Adam to the covenant of grace in Christ, grounded in the eternal covenant of redemption, the Bible tells one story of God keeping covenant with His people. The dictionary commends covenant theology as a faithful key to the whole of Scripture, exalting the faithfulness of the covenant-keeping God.

etymology: Dutch Reformed pastor (1635-1711) of the Further Reformation (Nadere Reformatie), author of The Christian's Reasonable Service.
biblical_def: Wilhelmus à Brakel was a Dutch Reformed pastor and a leading figure of the Nadere Reformatie, the Dutch Further Reformation that sought to carry the doctrines of the Reformation into the heart and life. His enduring work, The Christian's Reasonable Service (Redelijke Godsdienst, after Rom 12:1), is a vast and beloved manual of doctrine and devotion that walks the believer through the whole of theology and the Christian life with rare warmth and pastoral care. À Brakel writes not merely to inform the mind but to feed the soul, joining careful exposition of each doctrine to its practical use, its comfort, and its call to holiness. He was deeply concerned with the marks of true grace and the experience of communion with God, and his book became a household companion of Dutch piety for generations, read at the family hearth alongside the Scriptures. À Brakel stands in the dictionary as the great pastor-theologian of the Dutch Further Reformation, who taught the church that doctrine is for living, that the truths of grace are meant to be tasted and obeyed, and that the whole of theology bends toward the believer's reasonable service of a gracious God.

corruption_summary: À Brakel's legacy is honored by recovering experiential, practical theology — doctrine for the heart and life — against both dead orthodoxy and a shallow piety untethered from sound doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Head-heart divorce correction. Some imagine doctrine and devotion to be rivals: the precise are thought cold, the warm are thought shallow. À Brakel's great work joins them seamlessly, expounding each doctrine and then pressing its comfort and its call upon the soul. The dictionary holds that true theology is always for living; the knowledge of God is eternal life (John 17:3), and the deepest piety grows from the soundest doctrine, tasted and obeyed.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is experiential religion rightly defined — not feeling severed from truth, but the truth of God experienced in the conscience and life. À Brakel taught the believer to examine the marks of grace and to seek real communion with God. The dictionary commends his balance: a faith that is doctrinally sound, experimentally warm, and practically holy, presenting the body as a living sacrifice in reasonable service.

etymology: Dutch Reformed theologian (1589-1676), professor at Utrecht, a chief leader of the Further Reformation and a precise scholastic divine.
biblical_def: Gisbertus Voetius was a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at the University of Utrecht, one of the towering figures of seventeenth-century Reformed orthodoxy and a founder of the Nadere Reformatie. A delegate to the great Synod of Dort in his younger years, he became the most influential Dutch theologian of his generation, renowned for the breadth of his learning and the precision of his scholastic method. His Selectae Disputationes range across the whole field of theology and ethics with rigorous exactness. Voetius contended earnestly for orthodoxy on several fronts: against the looser covenant scheme of Cocceius, against the rising rationalism of Descartes, whose philosophy he judged a danger to faith, and against every laxity in doctrine and life. Yet his scholasticism was no mere intellectualism; he pressed for a living, practical godliness and for strict church discipline and personal holiness. Voetius stands in the dictionary as the great Utrecht scholastic and champion of Reformed orthodoxy, who wielded exact theological method in the service of the faith, defending sound doctrine against error and binding it always to the pursuit of holiness.
webster_summary: Dutch Reformed theologian (1589-1676), professor at Utrecht, a delegate to Dort and a leader of the Further Reformation; a precise scholastic who defended orthodoxy against Cocceius and Descartes and pressed for strict godliness.

corruption_summary: Voetius's legacy is honored by recovering the value of careful theological method and earnest contending for the faith, against an age that dismisses doctrinal precision as divisive and prizes vague sentiment over truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Precision-despised misreading. The modern temper often scorns theological exactness as needless hair-splitting and prizes a soft, undefined faith. Voetius shows the worth of precision: clear definitions guard the gospel, expose error, and protect the flock. The dictionary holds that earnestly contending for the faith once delivered (Jude 3) requires careful thought and exact words; the church that despises doctrinal precision soon loses the doctrine itself.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the union of orthodoxy and holiness. Voetius was no cold dogmatician; his rigorous theology served a passionate pursuit of godliness and disciplined church life. The dictionary commends his example against two errors at once: a precision without piety, and a piety without precision. Sound doctrine and strict holiness belong together, and Voetius held both with equal earnestness.

etymology: French-Dutch Reformed theologian (1545-1602), author of A Treatise on True Theology and co-translator of the Junius-Tremellius Latin Bible.
biblical_def: Franciscus Junius (François du Jon) was a French-born Reformed theologian who labored in the Netherlands and Germany, a scholar of great learning and irenic spirit. He is remembered for two lasting contributions. First, with Immanuel Tremellius he produced the Junius-Tremellius Latin translation of the Old Testament, long a standard scholarly Bible among Protestants. Second, in his A Treatise on True Theology, he gave classic expression to the Reformed distinction between archetypal and ectypal theology: the infinite, perfect knowledge that God has of Himself (archetypal), and the true but finite, accommodated knowledge that creatures receive by revelation (ectypal). This distinction, foundational to later Reformed orthodoxy, guards both the incomprehensibility of God and the genuineness of what He has revealed: we cannot know God as He knows Himself, yet what He graciously discloses is truly knowledge of Him. Junius was also a peacemaker who labored for concord among Protestants. He stands in the dictionary as a father of Reformed theological method, who taught the church that all our theology is a gift of revelation, true yet creaturely, and that the knowledge of God begins in humble reception of what the infinite God has stooped to make known.

corruption_summary: Junius's distinction guards against two errors: a rationalism that presumes to comprehend God as He is, and a skepticism that denies any true knowledge of God at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Rationalist presumption. Some imagine that the human mind can master the being of God, comprehending Him by reason as one object among others. Junius's archetypal/ectypal distinction humbles this presumption: God's knowledge of Himself is infinite and incommunicable; ours is finite, derived, and accommodated to our capacity. The dictionary holds the incomprehensibility of God — the secret things belong to Him — against every rationalism that would shrink the Infinite to the measure of the creature's understanding.

Skeptical despair. The opposite error concludes that, since we cannot know God exhaustively, we cannot truly know Him at all. Junius answers that ectypal theology, though finite, is true: what God reveals is real knowledge of Him, sufficient for faith and life. The dictionary holds the balance — the things revealed belong to us (Deut 29:29) — against both the pride that claims too much and the doubt that claims too little. We see through a glass darkly, yet we truly see.

etymology: Dutch Reformed theologian (1563-1641), the chief opponent of Arminius and a leading defender of predestination at the Synod of Dort.
biblical_def: Franciscus Gomarus was a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Leiden, remembered above all as the principal opponent of Jacobus Arminius and the standard-bearer of strict Calvinism in the controversy that led to the Synod of Dort (1618-1619). When Arminius and his followers (the Remonstrants) taught conditional election, resistible grace, and a universal intent in the atonement, Gomarus and his party (the Contra-Remonstrants or "Gomarists") contended for the unconditional, sovereign grace of God in salvation. The Synod of Dort vindicated their position, setting forth the doctrines later summarized as total depravity, unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints. Gomarus himself held the supralapsarian order of the divine decrees, though Reformed orthodoxy embraced both supra- and infralapsarian views within its bounds. A learned exegete and a vigorous controversialist, he gave his strength to defending the truth that salvation is of the Lord from first to last. Gomarus stands in the dictionary as the chief antagonist of Arminianism and a defender of sovereign grace, who labored that the church might confess God's free and unconditional election as the fountain of the believer's salvation.
webster_summary: Dutch Reformed theologian (1563-1641), the chief opponent of Arminius; leader of the Contra-Remonstrants whose defense of sovereign, unconditional grace was vindicated at the Synod of Dort.

corruption_summary: Gomarus's labor defends the doctrine of unconditional election against the Arminian scheme of conditional grace, and against every modern attempt to make salvation finally depend on the will of man rather than the mercy of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Conditional-election misreading. Arminianism, then and now, makes God's choice depend on foreseen faith or merit in the creature, so that salvation rests at last on man's will. Gomarus and the Synod of Dort answered from Scripture: God chose His people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them, but according to the good pleasure of His will (Eph 1:4-5). The dictionary holds unconditional election — salvation is not of him that willeth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16) — against every gospel that finally enthrones the human will.

On the lapsarian question, the dictionary notes that Reformed orthodoxy embraced both Gomarus's supralapsarianism and the more common infralapsarian view within its confessional bounds. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of grace itself, on which both views agree: election is unconditional, grace is effectual, and the Lamb's people are saved by the free and certain purpose of God. Gomarus's enduring service was not a particular order of decrees but the great confession that salvation is of the Lord.

etymology: Dutch Reformed theologian (1630-1706), author of Theoretical-Practical Theology, prized by Jonathan Edwards.
biblical_def: Petrus van Mastricht was a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor, the author of the great systematic work Theoretico-Practica Theologia (Theoretical-Practical Theology), which Jonathan Edwards judged better than any book except the Bible for a minister seeking divinity, esteeming it above even Turretin for its union of doctrine and life. Van Mastricht's method is itself his message: under each topic he sets out the exegesis of a key text, then the doctrine drawn from it, then its elenctic (polemical) defense against error, and finally its practical use for the conscience and life. Thus theory and practice are never divorced; every doctrine is traced from Scripture, guarded against error, and pressed upon the heart. The whole is ordered, comprehensive, and warm, a model of how Reformed scholasticism served godliness. Van Mastricht stands in the dictionary as the great theologian of theoretical-practical method, who taught the church that sound doctrine and holy living are one seamless garment, that every truth has its use, and that the end of all theology is that God be known, defended, and glorified in the life of His people.
webster_summary: Dutch Reformed theologian (1630-1706), author of Theoretical-Practical Theology, prized by Jonathan Edwards above all books but the Bible; modeled the union of exegesis, doctrine, polemics, and practice.

corruption_summary: Van Mastricht's method honors the recovery of theology as both true and useful, against a sterile academic divinity that never reaches the heart and a sentimental piety that never grounds itself in doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Theory-practice divorce correction. Modern divinity often splits into cold academic theology on one side and doctrineless devotion on the other. Van Mastricht's whole method refuses the split: every doctrine is exegeted from the text, defended against error, and applied to the life. The dictionary holds his pattern as the truth which is after godliness (Titus 1:1) — theology exists to be lived, and the soundest doctrine is the most practical, bending always toward holiness and the glory of God.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the practical end of all true theology. As the Lord said, "If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them" (John 13:17). Van Mastricht's great work shows that knowing and doing are not two enterprises but one; the dictionary commends his example to every student and minister, that doctrine learned might become obedience offered, and that all theology might issue in the worship of God.

etymology: Swiss Reformed theologian (1589-1629) of Basel, author of the widely used Compendium of Christian Theology.
biblical_def: Johannes Wollebius was a Swiss Reformed theologian of Basel, author of the Compendium Theologiae Christianae, one of the most concise, orderly, and widely used handbooks of Reformed theology in the seventeenth century. Where larger systems sprawled across many volumes, Wollebius distilled the whole of Christian doctrine into a clear, well-ordered summary, arranging it under the knowledge of God and the worship of God, and marking out the heads of doctrine with such precision that students across Europe and even in early New England learned their theology from him. His Compendium was prized for joining brevity to completeness: nothing essential omitted, nothing needless added, the great truths of the faith set in lucid order for ready learning and use. Wollebius represents the catechetical and pedagogical genius of Reformed orthodoxy, its concern that the doctrine of grace be not only defended in the academy but taught plainly to the rising generation. He stands in the dictionary as a master of theological compression, who served the church by setting the whole counsel of God in clear and memorable order, that pastors and people might grasp and hold the faith once delivered.

corruption_summary: Wollebius's example honors the recovery of clear, orderly instruction in doctrine, against an age that neglects the systematic teaching of the faith and leaves believers without a form of sound words.
corruption_paragraphs: Doctrine-disordered misreading. A faith taught only in fragments and impressions leaves believers unable to hold or defend the truth. Wollebius's gift was order: he set the whole of doctrine in clear arrangement, that it might be learned, remembered, and used. The dictionary holds the value of systematic instruction — a form of sound words (2 Tim 1:13) — against a piecemeal religion that never gives the believer the shape of the faith as a whole.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the catechetical handing-on of doctrine to the next generation. Wollebius wrote not for display but for teaching, that students and children might grasp the certainty of the things they had been taught (Luke 1:4). The dictionary commends his labor of compression and clarity: the church is bound to teach its children diligently, and clear, ordered doctrine is a gift to every generation that must learn the faith anew.

etymology: German-Swiss Reformed theologian (1561-1610) of Basel, author of the Syntagma Theologiae Christianae.
biblical_def: Amandus Polanus von Polansdorf was a German-Swiss Reformed theologian and professor at Basel, author of the Syntagma Theologiae Christianae, one of the major systematic theologies of early Reformed orthodoxy. Polanus arranged his system with the careful logical method of his age, working from clear definitions and orderly division to set forth the whole of Christian doctrine with thoroughness and precision. His treatment of the doctrine of God, of the divine attributes, and of the covenant was especially influential, and his work helped to shape the high orthodox theology that followed. Like the best of the Reformed scholastics, Polanus aimed not at speculation but at the faithful exposition and defense of the faith confessed in the Reformed churches, grounding doctrine in Scripture and ordering it for clarity and use. He stands in the dictionary as a builder of the Reformed systematic tradition, who labored to set the doctrine of God and His covenant in exact and reverent order, that the church might know its God truly and hold its confession firmly against the errors of the age.

corruption_summary: Polanus's labor honors the recovery of a high and ordered doctrine of God, against an age that shrinks the divine majesty to manageable, man-centered proportions.
corruption_paragraphs: God-diminished misreading. The modern temper often reduces God to a comfortable helper, His attributes softened to suit the creature's preferences. Polanus's careful doctrine of God recovers the biblical majesty: the great I AM, infinite in being and perfection, unsearchable in greatness, dwelling in unapproachable light. The dictionary holds that theology must begin with God as He has revealed Himself, exalted and holy, not as the creature would prefer Him, and commends the high doctrine of God the Reformed scholastics labored to preserve.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverent order in the knowledge of God. Polanus arranged the doctrine of God and the covenant with precision, not to confine the Infinite but to confess Him clearly and worship Him rightly. The dictionary commends such ordered theology: clear thinking about God, grounded in Scripture, is a servant of worship, leading the soul to adore the unsearchable greatness it cannot comprehend.

etymology: German Reformed theologian (1548-1622) of Heidelberg, biblical commentator and irenic advocate of Protestant concord.
biblical_def: David Pareus was a German Reformed theologian and professor at Heidelberg, a notable biblical commentator and a tireless advocate of unity among Protestants. A pupil of Zacharias Ursinus, he stood in the Heidelberg tradition of the great catechism, and labored to expound the Scriptures and defend Reformed doctrine in a turbulent age. His commentaries, especially on Romans and on the Revelation, were widely read; his work on Revelation shaped Protestant interpretation of the Apocalypse for generations. Pareus is also remembered for his Irenicum, a plea for concord between Lutheran and Reformed Protestants, seeking to heal the divisions that weakened the evangelical cause against Rome. His irenic spirit did not soften his Reformed convictions but sought to unite those who shared the great truths of the gospel. Pareus stands in the dictionary as a Heidelberg commentator and peacemaker, who labored both to expound the Word faithfully and to draw together the divided heirs of the Reformation, that the body of Christ might present a more united front for the truth of the gospel.
webster_summary: German Reformed theologian (1548-1622) of Heidelberg, a pupil of Ursinus; a biblical commentator (notably on Romans and Revelation) and irenic author of the Irenicum who sought concord among Protestants.

corruption_summary: Pareus's irenic labor honors the recovery of true Christian unity grounded in shared truth, against both a sectarian spirit that divides needlessly and a false ecumenism that unites by surrendering the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: False-ecumenism misreading. The modern ecumenical movement often pursues unity by minimizing doctrine, joining bodies that no longer share the gospel. Pareus sought no such hollow union; his Irenicum labored to unite those who held the great truths of the faith, not to paper over fundamental error. The dictionary holds that true unity is unity in the truth (John 17:17-21); to purchase concord by abandoning the gospel is not peace but treason against the One who is the Truth.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the opposite error's correction as well: a sectarian spirit that divides the godly over secondary matters. Pareus, firmly Reformed, still grieved the divisions that weakened the evangelical cause and sought to draw true brethren together. The dictionary commends his balance: hold the truth without compromise, yet labor for the unity of all who share it, that the world may believe.

etymology: Genevan Reformed theologian (1655-1724), nephew and successor of Francis Turretin, author of Christian Theology and Christian Ethics.
biblical_def: Benedict Pictet was a Genevan Reformed theologian, the nephew and academic successor of Francis Turretin, who carried the orthodox theology of Geneva into a warmer and more accessible register. Where his uncle's Institutes of Elenctic Theology was a rigorous scholastic and polemical work for the academy, Pictet's Christian Theology set forth the same Reformed faith in a clearer, more devotional, and more pastoral manner, for the edification of ordinary believers as well as students. He wrote likewise a notable Christian Ethics (or Christian Morals), applying the doctrines of grace to the whole conduct of the Christian life. Pictet labored at a time when the rigor of Genevan orthodoxy was beginning to give way to looser currents, and he sought to preserve the substance of the Reformed faith while commending it with gentleness and warmth. He stands in the dictionary as a bridge between the high orthodoxy of Turretin and the practical piety of the believing heart, who taught the church that the same sound doctrine defended in the schools is meant to be loved, lived, and enjoyed in communion with God, and who clothed the truths of grace in language ordinary saints could embrace.

corruption_summary: Pictet's work honors the recovery of sound doctrine commended with warmth and applied to the whole of life, against both a cold orthodoxy that never reaches the heart and a warm religion that never grounds itself in truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Doctrine-without-life misreading. Orthodoxy can harden into a merely intellectual exercise, defended in the schools but never loved or lived. Pictet took the rigorous theology of his uncle Turretin and clothed it in warmth, joining doctrine to ethics and devotion, that the truth might shape the conscience and conduct. The dictionary holds that the grace of God which brings salvation also teaches us to live soberly, righteously, and godly (Titus 2:11-12); sound doctrine is for holy living, not display.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the accessibility of sound doctrine to ordinary believers. Pictet refused to leave the riches of Reformed theology locked in the academy; he set them in language the believing heart could grasp and enjoy. The dictionary commends his example: the deepest truths of grace are meant for all the saints, and the faithful teacher labors to make them clear, that love may abound in knowledge and in all judgment (Phil 1:9).
